c.tagline: France's pink-brick 'Ville Rose', home of Airbus and the stars.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis run on the meter with a rooftop 'TAXI' sign; a night, Sunday, and airport surcharge applies. Booking by app or phone is common as street hailing is limited outside ranks.

emergency.note: 112 works Europe-wide; 17 reaches the police and 15 the medical SAMU service directly.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing/petty crime around Matabiau station and some peripheral areas

hood_desc: The monumental heart of the city around the grand Place du Capitole and its city hall, ringed by shops, brasseries, and the Basilica of Saint-Sernin nearby; best for first-timers wanting everything walkable.
A chic, tightly-woven quarter of pink-brick lanes, antique shops, the covered Marché des Carmes, and some of Toulouse's best restaurants; suits foodies and design-minded travellers.
The lively left bank across the Garonne, an arty, bohemian district with the Les Abattoirs modern-art museum, markets, and an easygoing local feel; good for a less touristy stay.
The riverside student quarter around Place Saint-Pierre, famous for its packed bar terraces and late-night crowd along the Garonne; the go-to base for nightlife.
The elegant, quieter cathedral district of grand hôtels particuliers, antique dealers, and leafy squares; suits travellers who want a calm, upscale corner of the centre.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout France.

transit.pay: A single Tisséo ticket is about €1.80 and a day pass around €6.80, sold at metro machines and tabac shops; the rechargeable Pastel card and contactless bank-card tap-in also work across metro, tram, and bus. The driverless VAL metro has two lines that intersect the whole network.
transit.hours: The metro runs roughly 5:15am to midnight, extended until around 3am on Friday and Saturday nights; buses run into the evening with weekend Noctambus night lines.

transit.m: Tram T2 to the city (Palais de Justice), ~30-40 min
Tisséo airport shuttle bus to Matabiau/centre, ~20-30 min

tip.r: Service is included by law ('service compris'); leaving a euro or two or rounding up for good service is a nice gesture but never required.

food.name: Cassoulet toulousain
food.desc: White tarbais beans baked for hours with Toulouse sausage, confit duck or goose and pork rind, served bubbling in its earthenware cassole.

places.name: Le Colombier
places.note: Open since 1924 and nicknamed the temple of cassoulet; goose confit and Toulouse sausage version.

places.name: Le Genty Magre
places.note: Chef Romain Brard won the 2023 cassoulet world championship; refined cooking in a small dining room.

places.name: Chez Emile
places.note: Founded in the 1940s, working from a 50-year-old house recipe on a beautiful central square.

food.name: Saucisse de Toulouse
food.desc: Coarse-ground pure pork sausage coiled and grilled, seasoned with little more than salt and pepper - the backbone of local cooking.

places.name: Marche Victor Hugo
places.note: The city's covered market; a dozen charcutiers sell the real coiled sausage by the metre.

places.name: Le Genty Magre
places.note: Cooks the sausage on its own as well as inside the cassoulet, with good local sourcing.

places.name: La Maison du Cassoulet
places.note: Southwest specialities including grilled Toulouse sausage and Castelnaudary-style cassoulet.

food.name: Garbure
food.desc: A thick Gascon soup of cabbage, beans, root vegetables and preserved duck - a meal in a bowl, eaten in winter across the southwest.

places.name: Chez Attila
places.note: One of the market's upstairs lunch restaurants cooking southwest classics from stalls below.

places.name: Le Magret
places.note: Duck-focused market restaurant; go at noon, the upstairs rooms only serve lunch.

places.name: La Maison du Cassoulet
places.note: Reliable for the wider Gascon repertoire alongside its signature cassoulet.

food.name: Magret de canard and foie gras
food.desc: Duck breast seared pink and sliced, or foie gras served terrine-style with Sauternes - the Gers and Landes just west supply Toulouse.

places.name: Marche Victor Hugo
places.note: Duck stalls sell everything from raw magret to confit; the upstairs restaurants cook it at lunch.

places.name: L'Os a Moelle
places.note: Neighbourhood address praised for its foie gras and traditional Toulouse cassoulet.

places.name: Chez Emile
places.note: Classic southwest menu with duck dishes and a deep regional wine cellar.

food.name: Violette de Toulouse sweets
food.desc: Crystallised violet petals, violet-flavoured chocolates, syrups and macarons - the city's emblem flower turned into confectionery.

places.name: La Maison de la Violette
places.note: Barge moored on the canal selling crystallised violets, syrups and liqueur; part shop, part museum.

places.name: Violettes et Pastels
places.note: Boutique devoted to violet and pastel sweets, good for gift boxes.

places.name: Marche Victor Hugo
places.note: Market confectioners stock violet sweets alongside other regional specialities.

food.name: Fenetra toulousain
food.desc: An old Toulouse tart: shortcrust with apricot jam and candied lemon under an almond meringue - sweet, chewy and hard to find outside the city.

places.name: Marche Victor Hugo
places.note: Market patissiers are among the few who still bake fenetra; ask at the pastry stalls.

places.name: Maison Pillon
places.note: Historic Toulouse chocolatier and patissier, a safe bet for local sweets and violet chocolates.

places.name: Bakeries around Place du Capitole
places.note: Several central patisseries make it seasonally alongside croustade and pastis gascon.

food.name: Fronton red wine
food.desc: Toulouse's own appellation, 20 km north, built on the local negrette grape - dark-fruited, violet-scented and drunk young.

places.name: N5 Wine Bar
places.note: Award-winning wine bar with a very large by-the-glass list including southwest appellations.

places.name: Le Temps des Vendanges
places.note: Small central wine bar and shop strong on Fronton, Gaillac and Madiran.

places.name: Marche Victor Hugo
places.note: Wine merchants in the market sell Fronton straight from the producers.

food.name: Liqueur de violette
food.desc: A pale purple, floral liqueur drunk neat over ice or splashed into sparkling wine - the drinkable version of the city's signature flower.

places.name: La Maison de la Violette
places.note: Sells the liqueur and syrup made from Toulouse violets, with tastings on the barge.

places.name: Violettes et Pastels
places.note: Stocks violet liqueur and syrup in gift sizes near the city centre.

places.name: N5 Wine Bar
places.note: Central bar where you can try it as an aperitif rather than buying a bottle.

landmarks: Basilica of Saint-Sernin
The largest surviving Romanesque church in Europe, this UNESCO-listed pink-brick basilica is Toulouse's spiritual and architectural crown jewel.
Capitole de Toulouse
The grand 18th-century pink facade of the city hall and opera house anchors the vast Place du Capitole, the beating heart of the 'Pink City'.
Pont Neuf (Toulouse)
Despite its name meaning 'new bridge,' this is Toulouse's oldest bridge, offering postcard views over the Garonne River and terracotta rooftops.
Couvent des Jacobins
A masterpiece of Gothic architecture famed for its 'palm tree' vaulted ceiling, this convent also holds the relics of Saint Thomas Aquinas.
Toulouse Cathedral (Cathédrale Saint-Étienne)
This quirky cathedral's mismatched nave and choir, built centuries apart, make it one of France's most architecturally curious sacred sites.
Hôtel d'Assézat
This Renaissance mansion, built on woad-dye fortunes, now houses academies and art collections behind an elegant courtyard facade.
Cité de l'Espace
A hands-on space exploration park featuring a full-scale Ariane rocket and planetarium that draws families and space enthusiasts alike.
Musée des Augustins
Housed in a former medieval convent, this fine arts museum's cloister and Romanesque sculpture collection are as striking as the artworks inside.
Canal du Midi
A UNESCO World Heritage waterway lined with plane trees, perfect for a scenic stroll, bike ride, or boat trip through the city.
Place Wilson
An elegant circular 19th-century square ringed with cafes and arcades, offering a lively spot to soak in local Toulousain life.

train.note: Toulouse Matabiau is the hub of south-west France, with TGV services to Paris in about 4h20 and Bordeaux in 2, plus Intercités to Marseille and the direct link toward Barcelona via Narbonne - check whether your service is direct or needs a change at the border. A high-speed line to Bordeaux is under construction. SNCF advance fares open around six months ahead.

bus.note: Coaches use the Gare Routière beside Matabiau station. Barcelona takes about 6 hours by coach and is often cheaper than the train; there are also direct services to Andorra la Vella in around 3h30, which has no railway of its own. Carry your passport or EU ID card.

ferry.note: Toulouse is inland on the Garonne and the Canal du Midi, neither of which carries scheduled passenger services - the canal boats are self-drive hire and hotel barges. There are no ferries.

half.name: Albi
half.blurb: Albi is a brick-built cathedral city on the Tarn River with the Toulouse-Lautrec museum in the former bishop's palace.

half.name: Carcassonne
half.blurb: Carcassonne is a fortified medieval city with double stone ramparts and turreted towers overlooking the Aude River.

half.name: Cordes-sur-Ciel
half.blurb: Cordes-sur-Ciel is a hilltop bastide town with stone Gothic houses and views over the Cerou valley.

half.name: Moissac
half.blurb: Moissac has a Romanesque abbey church with an intricately carved tympanum, a stop on the Camino de Santiago route.

half.name: Gaillac
half.blurb: Gaillac is a wine town on the Tarn River with vineyards dating to Roman times and a riverside old quarter.
